---
title: "Companies House: what it publishes and how to get it"
---

## Summary

Companies House is the UK's register of companies: it incorporates and dissolves companies,
records what they file, and publishes almost all of it. The register has been free to search
and download since 2015, and it is heavily used — billions of accesses a year. For an analyst,
four things matter: three free **bulk data products** (basic company data, the accounts
archive, and the daily PSC snapshot) plus a free **REST API** for current, per-company detail.
The important catch is that the API returns register fields but **not** parsed financial
figures — to get numbers out of accounts you still have to download and parse the filings
yourself, which is what this project does at scale.

For the low-level mechanics of each bulk product (file formats, where the historic archives
live, how often they refresh), [CH Guide](https://chguide.co.uk/) already documents them well,
and this guide links there rather than repeating them. The aim here is to explain what each
source *adds* for analysis and where it will surprise you.

## Details

### What Companies House is

Companies House is an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade. It is the
registrar for companies across England & Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Historically it
did very little checking of what companies filed; reforms under the **Economic Crime and
Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA)** are turning it from a passive record into a register
that verifies identities and can query or reject information. That transition is still rolling
out, so "verified" is not yet a safe assumption for older records.

A few figures give the scale:

| Figure | Value | Source & confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Companies on the register (31 March 2026) | 5.48m | CH annual report 2025/26. **[Checked]** |
| Times register data was accessed in 2025/26 | 14.6bn (16.3bn in 2024/25) | CH annual report 2025/26. **[Checked]** |
| Filings accepted in 2024/25 | 14.7m (13.5m digital) | CH annual report 2024/25. **[Checked]** |
| Estimated annual value to users | £1–3bn | 2019 study for CH/BEIS. **[Estimated]** (a study estimate) |

Source for all four: deck slide 3 and its notes, with primary sources listed in
`docs/source-material/companies-house-accounts-notes.md`.

> **What it means for you.** Free access since 2015 is why an open pipeline like this one is
> possible at all: the raw material costs nothing. Free accesses grew from 1.3bn in 2015/16 to
> over 16bn in 2023/24 (CH blog, June 2025; **[Checked]**).

### The three bulk products and the API

This is the practical core. Most analysts need only these four routes.

| Source | What's in it | Format & frequency | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Basic Company Data** | Live companies: name, number, status, registered office, SIC codes, key dates | CSV, monthly | Live companies only; no history. Keep monthly copies to reconstruct past states. |
| **Accounts bulk data** | Electronically filed annual accounts, tagged figure by figure | iXBRL/XML in ZIPs; daily and monthly, back to 2008 | E-filed only; mostly balance sheets (see below). |
| **PSC snapshot** | People and entities with significant control, plus statements | JSON, daily | Only *today's* file is served — archive your own copies or lose corrections over time. |
| **Officers bulk** | Directors and secretaries | On request only | Not a public bulk download. |
| **APIs** | REST: profiles, officers, PSC, filings, charges, insolvency. Streaming: live changes. Document API: filed documents | JSON; free key; rate-limited | **No parsed financial figures; no bulk history.** |

Source: deck slide 4 and its notes.

Two terms, with concrete examples:

- **iXBRL** ("inline XBRL"): an ordinary-looking HTML accounts page in which each figure is
  tagged with a machine-readable name — for example `<nonFraction name="Equity">12,968` tags
  the number 12,968 as the company's equity. A browser shows the page; a parser reads the tags.
  See [the accounts guide](accounts-data.qmd) for what this means in practice.
- **PSC**: a *person with significant control* — broadly, someone who owns or controls more
  than 25% of a company, or otherwise exerts significant influence. The daily snapshot is
  newline-delimited JSON, one record per line. See [the PSC status page](../datasets/psc.qmd).

> **What it means for you.** The API is the right tool for current, per-company state (status,
> overdue flags, insolvency links). It is the wrong tool for financials and for history: it
> returns no parsed numbers from accounts, and no bulk back-catalogue. That gap — API-for-state,
> bulk-download-plus-your-own-parser-for-financials — is the single most important thing to
> understand about getting data out of Companies House.

The published REST API rate limit is **about 600 requests per 5 minutes per key** (**[Not
verified]** — stated from the developer docs in deck slide 4's notes but not re-checked here;
confirm against the current [developer
documentation](https://developer-specs.company-information.service.gov.uk/)). This project's own
indicator pipeline deliberately runs below that (≈500/5min) because an API key may be shared
across tools — see [the indicators methodology](../indicators/methodology.qmd).

### Why we link to CH Guide instead of repeating it

[CH Guide](https://chguide.co.uk/) is a thorough, well-maintained explanation of Companies
House mechanics — the exact file layouts, the historic-archive pages back to 2008, the quirks
of each download. Re-documenting that here would duplicate work that is already done well and
would go stale faster than the original. So this guide links to CH Guide for mechanics and
concentrates on the layer above it: how the sources **join**, what each one **adds** for
analysis, and the [pitfalls](pitfalls.qmd) that only show up once you start using the data.
